name: Planographic stone lithography
summary: Printing from a flat, greased stone where ink sticks only to the oily image and not to the wet blank areas, letting music and pictures be printed without carving.
description: A level stone printing surface carries a greasy image and damp non-image areas; oily ink selectively adheres to the image, allowing impressions without incised or raised type.
tier_reason: A major reusable result, process or system within its field; broader multi-field or multi-generation dependence on this exact referent is not established.

impact.note: A new way to print drawn images, music and maps, used across many societies, from which chromolithography and offset printing grew as a line of work.

why: Senefelder was looking for a cheap way to reproduce his own plays and music; André, a music publisher, saw its value for printing scores.

market.note: The process can be supplied or used in economic production, separately from the date of its first offer.

date.label: 28 September 1799
date.basis: The city history reproduces a signed contract dated 28 September 1799; Senefelder reports that André paid 300 guilders at the agreement.

events.statement: In Munich, Anton André paid an advance for an agreement to acquire instruction in the entire stone-printing art and have a press set up.
events.scope: Paid access to the entire stone-printing art, including the level-surface method by scoped inference; instruction and press setup were promised for later.
events.population: Anton André as a music publisher
events.market: Anton André, music publisher and printer
events.caveats: The 1799 agreement covers the entire stone-printing art and promises instruction and a press; inclusion of the planographic branch follows from Senefelder’s account of its development and the contract’s breadth. Neither the 1799 demonstration nor any individual print is identified as level-surface rather than relief or intaglio. A 26 September notice offered stone printing generically but does not specify the planographic branch. The later 1800 Offenbach music production is separately documented; the first worldwide offer or sale is unresolved.
